doc.title: Mona Hinton interviewed by Milt Fillius and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995

title: Milt's photography and the S.S. Norway story
summary: Milt's candid photos taken on the road; darkroom with Keg Johnson, floods, and photographing sleepers, including the Hintons on the S.S. Norway.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Hunting for old band photographs and scrapbooks

blocks.x: I’d just wanted to ask you about, you know, Milt has this incredible collection of photos that is like an essay, a photo essay on jazz history. I wanted to ask you about that. As he was taking the pictures, and as you saw this compiling, did you realize that you were having that effect on jazz history?
No, not that single picture, but all the pictures he’s taken over the years.

Milton just loved to take pictures. On the road he and Keg Johnson, his dear friend, used to set up a darkroom in the bathroom in the theater or maybe the hotel where we were, and he took hundreds and hundreds of pictures. We never realized they would be that important because half the time he’d throw them in the drawers, and some of them had been taken and not developed for years. And then not only that we had a couple of floods in our basement and it wiped out a lot of our color photos and a lot of the other pictures. But they were just pictures. I mean he never in his wildest dreams ever dreamed that they would become this popular, or this important to the history of the music and the climate of our society, I mean in the United States in general. So I know that you’re familiar with the pictures of colored entrance and for colored only, and, but he was just taking pictures I mean for no particular reason other than the fact that he liked, and he’s not really a photographer you know, I mean he never studied photography or that kind of thing.
He’s better than most who have though.

Yes. He has frequently made this statement and it’s true that he’s been able to get a lot of pictures that the professional photographers couldn’t get because if a professional comes up, you know, you’re going to freeze or pose or something. Well he was one of the musicians in the studios or wherever they were, so he’s just snap, snap, snapping away, and I mean they wouldn’t pay him any attention. So that was why he was able to get a lot of pictures that are really very famous now and I think, of the people who eventually became legends in the business.
And catching people in very natural settings.

Exactly. Because I have to tell you a cute story. You know he takes pride in catching people asleep. So the year before last on the S.S. Norway they had us up so early to get off the ship and we waited and we waited and we waited and we waited. So there was a chaise lounge there, so he crawled up there and went to sleep. I was so tired I crawled up behind him and I went to sleep. Well I tell you they tell me the cameras were clicking like crazy. They finally got us. And I’m telling you I must have had twenty different photos of the two of us there sound asleep. That was to get back at us at that point.
